title: When Should a Leader Be Directive?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece lays out a practical framework for when good leaders should abandon their default facilitative style and simply tell people what to do. It identifies four conditions that justify directiveness: familiar crises, non-negotiable safety or ethical standards, sharply asymmetric expertise, and inexperienced team members who need guidance to build judgment. The article is careful to note that unfamiliar crises still benefit from a quick round of input before acting, since speed and novelty pull in different directions. It closes by stressing that the best leaders explain why they are being directive in the moment, which preserves trust even when they override normal collaborative process.
points: Good leaders default to facilitative styles but recognize specific conditions that call for directness instead.
Familiar crises reward fast, direct decisions, while unfamiliar crises still benefit from a quick check with others first.
Safety, ethics, and non-negotiable standards should not be opened to debate, even while explaining the reasoning.
Sharply asymmetric expertise and team member inexperience are the other two conditions that justify directiveness.
Explaining why a shift to directiveness is happening preserves trust that facilitative leadership has built.
quotes: They work hard to discuss, explore, and engage with people as opposed to simply telling them what to do.
The leader who insists on discussion while the building is on fire isn’t being inclusive; they’re being irresponsible.
While explaining the “why” behind the issue is required, inviting debate about it can send the wrong message.
A 'no' to all four means facilitate. A clear 'yes' to any one is a green light to be directive.
What they can’t accept is being told what to do by someone who doesn’t explain why their views aren’t necessary.
